title: More Than Words
objectives: I can name and explain ten words for playing with language, such as proverb, pun, and cliche.
I can tell the difference between slang, dialect, and a figure of speech.
I can use context clues to work out what a saying really means.
I can write about a symbol or saying that matters to me, using words from this unit.
rationale: Fifth graders meet sayings, jokes, and symbols in every book they read, but most cannot yet name what the author is doing. These ten words give students the labels (onomatopoeia, figure of speech, proverb, pun) and the language of everyday talk (slang, dialect, expression), plus three working verbs and nouns (cliche, symbolize, associate) for judging how fresh or how meaningful a phrase is. The unit follows the unit 1 connotation work: a word can feel different from its dictionary meaning, and a saying can mean something different from its words. Students leave able to say that a phrase is figurative, name the kind, and explain what it really means. Dignity, noble, and viewpoint are revisited because symbols and sayings so often carry a viewpoint or a value.

words.def: A word that sounds like the noise it names, such as buzz.
words.ex: The word sizzle is onomatopoeia because you can almost hear bacon in the pan.
words.ex2: Comic book artists love onomatopoeia, so their pages explode with words like boom and zap.
words.nonExample: The word table is not onomatopoeia, since it makes no sound.
words.rel: words that sound like what they mean

apps.academic: Poets use onomatopoeia to help readers hear the scene.
apps.spoken: My sister's poem is full of onomatopoeia, like splash and plop.
apps.writing: Use onomatopoeia when you want the reader to hear a sound in the sentence.

cloze.s: The word thud is a good example of ___, because it sounds like a heavy object hitting the floor.

cloze2.s: A poem full of words like clang, hiss, and murmur uses ___ to bring the sounds alive.

misuse.s: The word table is onomatopoeia because it sounds just like a table.
misuse.why: Onomatopoeia imitates a sound, and the word table does not imitate any noise.

visual.alt: A bee with the words buzz and boom bursting around it.

words.def: A creative phrase that means something different from its plain, literal words.
words.ex: Saying a test was a piece of cake is a figure of speech, not a talk about dessert.
words.ex2: The poet used a figure of speech when she wrote that the moon was a silver coin.
words.nonExample: Saying that a cake has three layers is not a figure of speech.
words.rel: words that mean more than they say

apps.academic: Authors use a figure of speech to make a picture in the reader's mind.
apps.spoken: When my brother said he was starving, I knew it was only a figure of speech.
apps.writing: Use a figure of speech sparingly so that each one stands out.

cloze.s: "Raining cats and dogs" is a ___ because no animals are really falling from the sky.

cloze2.s: When Dad said the traffic was a zoo, he used a ___ to say it was wild and crowded.

misuse.s: When she said her backpack weighed a ton, it was a figure of speech, so the bag really weighed two thousand pounds.
misuse.why: A figure of speech is not literal; the backpack only felt very heavy.

visual.alt: A speech bubble with a lightning bolt, showing words that mean more than they say.

words.frame: The figure of speech ___ really means ___.

words.def: A short, well-known saying that gives advice or states a truth.
words.ex: My grandfather often quotes the proverb "Slow and steady wins the race."
words.ex2: Every culture has a proverb about the value of patience.
words.nonExample: A weather report on the radio is not a proverb.

apps.academic: A proverb often uses a simple picture to teach a lesson.
apps.spoken: My aunt answers every problem with a proverb.
apps.writing: Use a proverb in an essay to open or close with a lesson most readers know.

cloze.s: The ___ "Look before you leap" warns us to think before we act.

cloze2.s: Because that old ___ about patience helped the family through hard times, they repeated it often.

misuse.s: The proverb was a long, funny story that nobody had heard before.
misuse.why: A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice, not a long new story.

visual.alt: A scroll with a needle and thread, for a saying about fixing things early.

words.frame: One proverb I know is ___, which means ___.

words.def: A joke that plays on a word with two meanings or sounds.
words.ex: The baker's pun about needing more dough made the whole line of customers groan.
words.ex2: Her sign read "Lettuce be friends," a pun on the word let us.
words.nonExample: A riddle with only one meaning is not a pun.

apps.academic: A pun works because one word is used in two ways at once.
apps.spoken: My dad cannot hear a word without making a pun on it.
apps.writing: Use a pun in a title to add humor, but check that both meanings are clear.

cloze.s: The shop called "Sew What?" is a ___ because sew sounds like so and means to stitch.

cloze2.s: The comedian's ___ about the clock was about time, and the audience laughed when they saw the second meaning.

misuse.s: The pun was not funny at all because it had only one meaning.
misuse.why: A pun needs two meanings or sounds; a single meaning is not a pun.

visual.alt: A smiling face above two meanings of one word.

words.frame: A pun I could make about ___ is ___.

words.def: Casual, informal words that friends use and that change quickly.
words.ex: The new slang my cousins use is hard for my grandparents to understand.
words.ex2: She uses slang with her team but speaks formally in a debate.
words.nonExample: A formal speech to the city council is not slang.

apps.academic: A reporter may quote a person's slang, but the article itself uses standard English.
apps.spoken: I use slang when I text my friends.
apps.writing: Avoid slang in a formal report, because readers may not know it or it may sound out of date.

cloze.s: Last year's ___ already sounds old, because the casual words kids use keep changing.

cloze2.s: When the principal spoke to the visitors, he used no ___, only careful and formal language.

misuse.s: The judge's formal speech was full of slang that she picked up from her friends.
misuse.why: Slang is casual language among friends, so it does not fit a formal courtroom speech.

visual.alt: A cool face with a casual speech bubble.

words.def: A form of a language spoken by people in one place or group.
words.ex: Each region of the country has its own dialect, with different words for the same thing.
words.ex2: The poet wrote part of the story in the dialect of her island village.
words.nonExample: A language learned from a book alone is not a dialect.
words.rel: how a place or group speaks

apps.academic: Linguists study the dialect of a region to learn how its speech changed.
apps.spoken: My cousins from the South have a dialect that I love to hear.
apps.writing: When you write dialogue, use dialect carefully so every reader can understand it.

cloze.s: The people from the mountain town spoke a ___ with words that visitors had never heard.

cloze2.s: In the old story, the sailor's ___ made it clear that he came from the coast.

misuse.s: A dialect is a mistake in grammar that a good speaker avoids.
misuse.why: A dialect is a normal form of a language used by a group, not a mistake.

visual.alt: A map with speech bubbles from different regions.

words.frame: The dialect in ___ has a word for ___.

words.def: A phrase used so often that it has lost its freshness.
words.ex: "Busy as a bee" is a cliche that many writers avoid.
words.ex2: The movie was full of cliche, from the hero walking away from an explosion to the villain's evil laugh.
words.nonExample: A brand new comparison that no one has used before is not a cliche.

apps.academic: Editors often mark a cliche and ask writers for a fresh image.
apps.spoken: My teacher circled "quiet as a mouse" and wrote cliche beside it.
apps.writing: Replace a cliche with a detail only you would notice.

cloze.s: "It was a dark and stormy night" is a ___ that has opened too many stories.

cloze2.s: The writer replaced the ___ "white as snow" with a fresh comparison no one had heard before.

misuse.s: The speaker used a fresh, never-heard-before comparison, so everyone called it a cliche.
misuse.why: A cliche is an overused phrase, not a fresh new one.

visual.alt: A speech bubble with a circular arrow, showing a phrase used again and again.

words.frame: A cliche I hear a lot is ___.

words.def: To stand for or represent an idea.
words.ex: In the story, the broken clock seemed to symbolize the family's lost time together.
words.ex2: On the flag, the stars symbolize each state, so adding a state means adding a star.
words.nonExample: A rock sitting on a path does not symbolize anything unless the author gives it meaning.

segs.m: something that stands for something else

apps.academic: Authors use an object to symbolize a theme such as freedom or loss.
apps.spoken: I think the green light symbolizes hope in that scene.
apps.writing: When you write about a symbol, say what it is and what it symbolizes.

cloze.s: In many cultures a white dove is chosen to ___ peace, so it appears on posters about ending war.

cloze2.s: The artist painted a tall tree to ___ the strength of the family, with deep roots and many branches.

misuse.s: A red stop sign cannot symbolize anything because it is just a color.
misuse.why: A stop sign symbolizes the order to stop; a symbol stands for an idea.

visual.alt: A dove carrying a green branch.

words.def: To connect one thing with another in your mind.
words.ex: I associate the smell of cinnamon with my grandmother's kitchen.
words.ex2: Many people associate the sound of an ice cream truck with summer.
words.nonExample: Writing a word on the board is not the same as associating it with a feeling.

apps.academic: Scientists may associate certain weather with changes in animal behavior.
apps.spoken: I always associate that song with my road trip.
apps.writing: Use associate to show a link a person makes in the mind, not a fact.

cloze.s: Because she sang there every summer, she would always ___ that lake with happy memories.

cloze2.s: Many students ___ the first week of fall with sharpened pencils and new notebooks.

misuse.s: I associate the number seven with the color blue, so it means seven is made of blue paint.
misuse.why: Associate means to link in the mind; it does not mean made of.

visual.alt: A brain connected by a chain link to a picture.

words.def: A word or phrase used to say something in a colorful way.
words.ex: "Break a leg" is an expression that actors use to wish each other good luck.
words.ex2: Grandpa has an expression for every kind of weather, and my favorite is "fine as frog hair."
words.nonExample: A silent look on someone's face is not a spoken expression.
words.rel: a phrase with a special flavor

apps.academic: Every language has expressions that cannot be translated word for word.
apps.writing: Use an expression to give your writing a human voice, but explain it if readers might not know it.

cloze.s: The ___ "under the weather" means feeling a little sick, not standing beneath clouds.

cloze2.s: A person new to English may find the ___ "hit the books" confusing, since it has nothing to do with hitting.

misuse.s: An expression is a number that you add or subtract in a math problem.
misuse.why: In this unit an expression is a word or phrase said in a colorful way, not a math problem.

visual.alt: A speech bubble with sparkles, showing a colorful phrase.

words.frame: An expression my family uses is ___.

passage.title: The Saying Collector
paras: Marisol's grandmother never says a plain thing when a colorful one will do. After a loud thunderstorm that left only a few drops of rain, she shrugged and said, "All bark and no bite." Marisol was collecting sayings for a class project, so she wrote it down at once. Her teacher, Ms. Okafor, had asked everyone to find one figure of speech from home and explain what it really means.

At school, Dev brought the proverb "A stitch in time saves nine," which his uncle says whenever a button comes loose. Priya shared a pun: "Why did the pencil go to the meeting? It wanted to get to the point." The class groaned and laughed at the same time. Then Jamal read a line from a comic book, "Buzz, whirr, clank," and Ms. Okafor explained that every word was onomatopoeia, because each one sounds like the noise it names.

Not every saying earned a place on the poster. "Cool as a cucumber" was a cliche, Ms. Okafor said, because everyone had heard it a thousand times. Slang was trickier. The casual words friends use change so quickly that last year's favorite can sound out of date. Marisol's grandmother speaks a dialect with words that her classmates had never heard, and the class decided those sayings were treasures.

Finally, Marisol drew a white bird on the cover. "A dove can symbolize peace," she said, "and I associate it with my grandmother's garden." Ms. Okafor smiled. "Every expression carries a picture, a feeling, and a history," she said.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "cliche" most nearly means a phrase that is
choices: so old and overused that it has lost its freshness
new and shocking to most listeners
only spoken in one part of the country
too difficult for children to understand
qs.why: Ms. Okafor says everyone had heard "cool as a cucumber" a thousand times, so a cliche is a worn-out, overused phrase.

qs.q: What does Marisol's grandmother mean by "All bark and no bite" after the storm?
choices: A dog had barked all night during the storm.
The storm was loud but did very little.
The rain was cold enough to hurt.
The thunder frightened the neighbors.
qs.why: The storm was loud but left only a few drops, so it made a lot of noise and did little, like a dog that barks but never bites.

qs.q: Why did Ms. Okafor call Jamal's comic book line onomatopoeia?
choices: It rhymed with another line in the book.
It was a joke with two meanings.
Each word sounded like the noise it named.
It was an old saying with advice in it.
qs.why: The text says every word was onomatopoeia because each one sounds like the noise it names.

qs.q: Why did the class treat the grandmother's sayings as treasures?
choices: They were all clever puns.
They were a different way of speaking that no one else in the class knew.
They had been printed in a famous book.
They were the easiest sayings to explain.
qs.why: The class had never heard her dialect words and decided the sayings were valuable, not wrong, because they were different and special.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Sayings, jokes, and symbols let a few words carry much more than they seem to say.
Proverbs are always better than puns.
A good project needs a poster with a bird on it.
Grandmothers speak more colorfully than teachers.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows a kind of language play, and Ms. Okafor ends by saying every expression carries a picture, a feeling, and a history.

write.prompt: Write about a saying, joke, or symbol from your family or community. Explain what it really means. Use at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: In my family, people say ___, which means ___. I associate it with ___.

study.task: Sort the ten words into two piles: names for kinds of language play (such as pun or proverb) and words for how language is used or judged (such as cliche or dialect). Choose one saying you know and tell which pile word fits it best and why.

choices: proverb : saying
slang : formal
buzz : bee
dialect : map
cliche : overused
symbolize : picture
proverb : advice
pun : serious

sentences: Write a sentence that uses proverb and gives the advice the proverb offers.
Write a pun of your own and then use the word pun to say why it is funny.

given: The story was full of the same old phrases.
Every character was "cool as a cucumber."
combine.model: Mia's story was full of cliche, since every character was cool as a cucumber.
Artists often use a heart to symbolize love and a skull to symbolize danger.

discuss: Is it ever good to use a cliche? When might an old saying be the right choice?
Why might a person use slang with friends but not in a job interview?
Which has more power to teach, a proverb or a long explanation? Defend your choice.
produce.explain: Explain the difference between a pun and a proverb. Give one example of each and tell what makes each one work.

argue.prompt: Claim: Students should learn old proverbs even though some sound old-fashioned. Take a side and give two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe students should / should not learn proverbs because ___. A proverb is useful when ___.

constructed.prompt: Write two or three sentences. One sentence should show a pun about something at school. Another should name a word that is onomatopoeia and tell what noise it names.
look: gives a joke with a true double meaning
names a word that sounds like its noise
constructed.model: A pun about school: Why was the math book sad? It had too many problems. The word crash is onomatopoeia because it sounds like the noise of something falling and breaking.

constructed.prompt: Choose an animal, color, or object that symbolizes something to you. Tell what it stands for, what you associate with it, and one expression that goes with it.
look: uses symbolize, associate, and expression correctly
names a clear object and what it stands for
constructed.model: A red cardinal symbolizes my grandfather to me. I associate it with winter mornings when he filled the bird feeder. He used to say the expression "early bird" whenever we woke up early to watch it.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for talking about language itself: the named kinds of figurative language, the way people talk in different groups, and the verbs that explain how words carry meaning. The passage is a school story in which students collect sayings, which keeps the focus on what each saying really means. Writing asks students to explain a saying or symbol from their own lives.

notes.va.onomatopoeia.n: Say it slowly in syllables and let students clap them (on-o-mat-o-PEE-uh). The idea is simple: the word imitates the sound. Collect examples from comics and have students sort real onomatopoeia from words that merely describe sound.
notes.va.figure-of-speech.phr: This is the umbrella term: pun, proverb, and cliche sit under language that is not meant literally. Always ask what the phrase literally says and what it really means. Students who read literally often miss the real meaning, so model both readings.
notes.va.proverb.n: A proverb is short, well known, and gives advice. Not every saying is a proverb: Cool as a cucumber describes, but a stitch in time saves nine advises. Ask students for proverbs from their own families and languages.
notes.va.pun.n: A pun depends on two meanings or two sounds colliding. Students can see a joke but not explain it, so have them draw both meanings. The explanation is the learning.
notes.va.slang.n: Slang is informal and changes fast. Avoid calling it wrong. Teach that people choose language for the audience, which is a skill, not a defect. Compare slang to dialect: slang is about informality, dialect is about a place or group.
notes.va.dialect.n: A dialect is a full, rule-governed form of a language. Take care that students do not treat one dialect as correct and others as broken. Invite students to share words from their own homes and regions respectfully.
notes.va.cliche.n: A cliche is a phrase that was once fresh and is now worn out. The pronunciation (klee-SHAY) is borrowed from French. Have students rewrite a cliche with a fresh comparison and compare the two.
notes.va.symbolize.v: Students often say a symbol is the thing, not what it stands for. Model: a dove is a bird, but it symbolizes peace. Use traffic signs, flags, and colors, then move to literature.
notes.va.associate.v: The sense taught here is connect in the mind. Students may also know it as a coworker or a verb meaning spend time with someone. Keep the taught sense: Model with a personal connection, such as I associate rain with the smell of wet grass.
notes.va.expression.n: Expression has several senses, including a look on a face. Here it means a word or phrase with a special flavor, as in a common expression. Ask students to say which sense they hear in each example.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The grandmother says all bark and no bite after a loud storm with few raindrops. A dog does not appear in this story, so the phrase cannot be literal. A dog that barks loudly but never bites is noisy but harmless, and the storm was noisy but harmless. So this is a figure of speech, and its real meaning is loud but not dangerous.'
discuss: Which of the ten words names something you meet in your reading, and which names something you hear in your own life?
Why might two people from different regions use different words for the same thing, and what does that tell us about dialect?
misconceptions: Slang and dialect mean the same thing.
A cliche is always a bad phrase; students may think cliches are wrong rather than just overused.
A symbol is the same as the thing it stands for.
Every funny sentence is a pun; a pun needs two meanings.
extend: Make a class poster of onomatopoeia from comics, sorted by the kind of noise.
Have students translate a proverb from another language and compare its picture with an English proverb about the same advice.
Rewrite a cliche from a favorite story with a fresh comparison of your own.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit viewpoint, dignity, and noble by asking what a symbol or saying says about a person's viewpoint or values, such as a flag that stands for a noble idea. Return to the sort of language play words after two days, again at one week, using sayings from the students' own homes.

frames: The saying ___ does not really mean ___; it means ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says a saying from home or a favorite book. Partner B tells what the words say and what they really mean, then names which word from the unit fits it best.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: figura retórica for figure of speech (not a single standard term), proverbio for proverb (refrán is the more common everyday word), jerga for slang (jerga and argot overlap), juego de palabras for pun.

Proverb and pun examples in the passage (a stitch in time saves nine; the pencil pun; cool as a cucumber; all bark and no bite) are common sayings or original jokes with no factual claim; not checked against a source.
Dove as a symbol of peace is a widely used convention, stated in the passage as 'can symbolize', not as a universal rule.
